name: Preppy

influenced_by: actual Ivy League and Northeastern boarding-school dress codes

eras: mid-20th century, codified 1980 (The Official Preppy Handbook)

media.title: Lisa Birnbach (ed.), The Official Preppy Handbook (1980)
media.note: the book that named and satirized the style for a mass audience

reacts_against: 1970s countercultural dressing-down, reclaiming a visibly formal, old-money-coded wardrobe at a moment when casualness had become the more rebellious choice.
revivals: Ralph Lauren's ongoing commercial reinterpretation since the 1970s-80s
article: Preppy style is unusual in having an exact, dateable codification: The Official Preppy Handbook, edited by Lisa Birnbach and published in 1980, took the real dress codes of elite Northeastern prep schools and Ivy League colleges and turned them into a best-selling satirical guide — simultaneously mocking the style and, by giving it a name and a shopping list, making it far easier for people outside that world to buy into it. The book arrived at a moment when 1970s countercultural dressing-down had made visible formality itself feel like the more unexpected choice, and Ralph Lauren's parallel commercial build-out of Ivy-coded branding through the same period turned a once-exclusive campus uniform into a widely available retail category. The style's pastel argyle, boat shoes and popped collars have cycled in and out of fashion-media attention repeatedly since, most recently absorbed into the 2020s "old money" and quiet-luxury trend wave, which keeps preppy's palette while dropping most of its original collegiate specificity.

findings: mostly muted — about 59% of the measured color is low-saturation (greys, dusty tones)
